questions: How has technology changed the way people communicate?
Do you think people depend too much on technology?
Is it important for older people to learn how to use new technology?
What are the disadvantages of new technology?
What new technology do you think will change our lives the most in the future?
sampleAnswers: It's transformed it completely. We can now communicate instantly with almost anyone in the world, often for free, and video calls allow families separated by distance to see each other regularly. Communication has also become much more constant; we're always connected through messaging apps and social media. However, some people argue that the quality of communication has suffered. Conversations are often shorter and more superficial, and many people seem more comfortable texting than talking face to face, which can make real-life interactions feel more awkward.

To some extent, yes. Many people would struggle to navigate a city without a map app or remember phone numbers without their contacts list. This dependence becomes obvious when there's a power cut or the internet goes down, and everything grinds to a halt. Having said that, depending on technology isn't necessarily a bad thing. We've always depended on tools, from the printing press to electricity. The real problem arises when it affects our health or relationships, for example when people can't put down their phones even during meals with friends.

Yes, I'd say it's increasingly important. So many essential services, such as banking, booking medical appointments or accessing government information, have moved online, and older people who can't use technology risk being excluded or becoming dependent on others. It can also help them stay in touch with family and reduce loneliness. However, I think the responsibility shouldn't fall entirely on older people. Companies and governments should make services simpler and continue to offer alternatives, like phone lines or in-person help, for those who struggle.

One major disadvantage is the impact on our attention and mental health. Many apps are designed to be addictive, and constant notifications make it hard to concentrate. Privacy is another serious concern, as companies collect huge amounts of personal data, often without users fully understanding how it's used. There's also an environmental cost, since devices require rare materials and are often replaced after just a few years. Finally, technology can widen inequality, because those without access or skills are left further behind.

I suspect artificial intelligence will have the biggest impact. It's already being used in areas like medicine, where it can help detect diseases earlier, and it could transform education by offering personalised learning to every student. On the other hand, it may also replace many jobs, so societies will need to think carefully about how to manage that transition. Another technology with enormous potential is renewable energy storage, such as better batteries, which could make clean energy far more reliable and help tackle climate change.

questions: Why do you think documentaries have become more popular recently?
Can films influence the way people think and behave?
Should films that are shown in schools be educational or entertaining?
Do you think going to the cinema will become less common in the future?
How reliable do you think documentaries are as a source of information?
sampleAnswers: I think streaming platforms have played a huge role. They've invested heavily in documentaries and made them easily accessible, so people can discover them without much effort. Production quality has also improved dramatically, so many documentaries now feel as gripping as a thriller. There's also a growing interest in real stories, particularly true crime and environmental topics. Perhaps in a world full of fiction and social media, people are looking for content that feels authentic and helps them understand complex issues.

Yes, I think they can be very influential, although usually in subtle ways. Films can shape our attitudes towards certain groups of people, for example by challenging or reinforcing stereotypes. They can also raise awareness of social issues; some documentaries have led to real changes in consumer behaviour or even government policy. Of course, people aren't passive, and most can distinguish between fiction and reality. But when we see a particular image repeated across many films, it can gradually affect what we consider normal.

Ideally, both. If a film is purely educational but dull, students will switch off and learn very little. On the other hand, a purely entertaining film might be a waste of valuable class time. The best option is probably a film that's engaging but also relates to what students are studying, such as a historical drama or a well-made science documentary. The key, I think, is what the teacher does afterwards. A good discussion can turn even an entertaining film into a valuable learning experience.

It's quite likely, given how convenient streaming is. Many people now have large televisions and good sound systems at home, and a cinema trip can be expensive, especially for families. However, I doubt cinemas will disappear entirely. Watching a film on a huge screen with a crowd is a social experience that's hard to replicate at home, and big blockbusters still attract large audiences. Cinemas may have to adapt, perhaps by offering more comfortable seating, special events or a better food experience, to give people a reason to leave home.

I think they can be quite reliable, but viewers should be cautious. Documentaries are made by people with particular perspectives, and filmmakers have to select what to include and what to leave out, which inevitably shapes the message. Some documentaries are carefully researched and balanced, while others are closer to persuasive films designed to convince the audience of a particular argument. So I'd say they're a good starting point for learning about a topic, but it's wise to check other sources, especially for controversial subjects.

questions: In what ways do people in your country help each other?
Why are some people unwilling to help strangers?
Should people be rewarded for helping others?
Is it more important to help people in your own community or people in other countries?
How can cities be designed to help people feel more connected to each other?
sampleAnswers: In many ways. Within families, help is very common; grandparents often look after their grandchildren so parents can work, and adult children care for their elderly parents. In smaller communities, neighbours tend to look out for each other, for example by keeping an eye on someone's house when they're away. There's also quite a strong tradition of volunteering, especially with organisations like food banks and the Red Cross. And when there's a natural disaster, people usually respond very generously with donations.

I think the main reasons are fear and uncertainty. People may worry that the situation could be dangerous or that the person might take advantage of them. There's also what psychologists call the bystander effect: when there are lots of people around, everyone assumes someone else will help. Busy lifestyles play a part too; people are often in a hurry and don't notice when someone needs assistance. And in some cases people simply aren't sure how to help, so they do nothing rather than risk doing the wrong thing.

I'm not sure that rewards are the right approach in most cases. If people help others mainly to receive something in return, it might undermine the genuine kindness behind it. However, I think public recognition can be positive. Highlighting acts of kindness in the media or giving awards to outstanding volunteers can inspire others. Also, for long-term volunteering that requires a lot of time, offering things like training or academic credit seems fair, because it makes volunteering possible for people who couldn't otherwise afford the time.

That's a difficult one, and I don't think there's a simple answer. On the one hand, helping your local community has visible, immediate effects, and you understand the problems better. On the other hand, the needs in some other parts of the world are far more urgent; a small donation can have a much greater impact where poverty is extreme. Personally, I think a balance is sensible. People could volunteer their time locally, where being physically present matters, while supporting international causes financially.

I think public spaces are key. Parks, squares and pedestrian streets where people can meet casually encourage interaction in a way that busy roads don't. Community centres, libraries and local markets also bring people together. Housing design matters too; buildings with shared gardens or common areas can help neighbours get to know each other. Some cities are also creating neighbourhoods where everything you need is within a short walk, which means people are more likely to bump into each other and build relationships.

questions: Why do you think so many people enjoy watching sport?
Do you think professional athletes are paid too much?
What can governments do to encourage people to exercise more?
Are major sporting events, like the Olympics, good for the countries that host them?
How has technology changed sport?
sampleAnswers: I think sport offers drama and unpredictability that's hard to find elsewhere. Unlike a film, nobody knows how a match will end, which creates real tension and excitement. There's also a strong sense of belonging. Supporting a team gives people a shared identity and a reason to connect with friends, family and even strangers. For many people, it's also a form of escapism from everyday problems. And of course, watching athletes perform at an extraordinary level can be genuinely inspiring.

In some sports, the salaries do seem excessive, especially compared with essential workers like nurses or teachers. However, I can understand why it happens. Top athletes generate huge amounts of money for their clubs through ticket sales, broadcasting rights and advertising, so in market terms, they're simply getting a share of what they bring in. Also, their careers are usually short, and only a tiny percentage reach the top. So while the figures can feel unfair, I'm not sure it's easy to change without restricting the market.

Probably the most effective thing is to make exercise easy and affordable. That might mean building more public sports facilities, creating safe cycling lanes, and keeping parks well maintained. Governments could also subsidise sports clubs for children and low-income families. Schools play a crucial role too; if children develop a love of exercise early, they're more likely to stay active as adults. Public campaigns can raise awareness, but I suspect changing the physical environment has a much bigger impact than advertising.

It depends very much on how well they're planned. They can bring benefits like improved infrastructure, more tourism and a boost to national pride. However, they're extremely expensive, and some host countries have been left with enormous debts and stadiums that are hardly used after the event. Local residents are sometimes displaced to make room for new facilities. So I'd say they can be beneficial if a country uses existing venues and plans for long-term use, but otherwise they may cost more than they deliver.

Technology has had a huge impact. Equipment has become lighter and more efficient, which has helped athletes break records. Video technology now helps referees make fairer decisions, although it's also caused controversy because it can slow the game down. Training has become much more scientific, with athletes using data from wearable devices to monitor their performance and avoid injuries. For fans, technology has made it possible to watch almost any event live from anywhere in the world, which has turned some sports into truly global industries.

questions: Why is it important to learn about history?
Do you think history is taught in an interesting way in schools?
Should historical sites be free for everyone to visit?
How can technology help people learn about history?
Is tourism a threat to historical places?
Do you think future generations will be interested in our present time?
sampleAnswers: History helps us understand why the world is the way it is today. Many current conflicts, political systems and cultural traditions only make sense when you know their background. It can also help us avoid repeating past mistakes, although I'm not sure humanity always learns those lessons. On a personal level, history gives people a sense of identity and belonging. And studying history develops valuable skills, such as analysing different sources and understanding that events can be interpreted from very different perspectives.

Not always, in my experience. Too often, it's taught as a list of dates, kings and battles to be memorised, which can make it feel quite irrelevant to students' lives. However, I think this is changing in many schools. Some teachers now use primary sources, role-plays and local history projects, which make the subject much more engaging. Learning about how ordinary people lived, rather than just famous leaders, also helps students relate to the past. Visits to museums and historical sites can make a huge difference too.

I think there's a strong argument for keeping them free or at least very affordable, because heritage belongs to everyone, and high prices can exclude people on lower incomes. However, maintaining historical sites is extremely expensive, and entrance fees are often an important source of funding. One possible compromise is to charge foreign tourists while keeping access free for local residents or students. Another option is to have free entry on certain days. That way, the sites can be maintained without becoming accessible only to the wealthy.

Technology offers some exciting possibilities. Virtual reality can recreate ancient cities or historical events, allowing people to experience what life might have been like. Augmented reality apps can show visitors how a ruined building originally looked while they're standing in front of it. Digitising archives also means that researchers and the public can access historical documents from anywhere. The risk, perhaps, is that some reconstructions involve a lot of guesswork, so it's important to make clear what's based on evidence and what's imagined.

It can be, if it isn't managed properly. Large numbers of visitors can physically damage fragile sites, for example by wearing down stone floors or touching delicate surfaces. Popular places can also become so crowded that they lose their atmosphere. However, tourism also provides the money and the motivation to preserve these places; without visitors, many sites might be neglected. So I think the solution lies in careful management, such as limiting visitor numbers, using timed tickets and closing particularly vulnerable areas.

I imagine they will be, probably in ways we can't predict. Our era will likely be seen as a period of enormous technological change, especially the rise of the internet and artificial intelligence, as well as the climate crisis. Ironically, though, future historians might struggle to understand us, because so much of our information is stored digitally and could be lost if formats become obsolete. They might find it easier to study a medieval manuscript than a website from twenty years ago, which is a slightly worrying thought.

questions: Why do people today seem busier than in the past?
Is it possible to have a good work-life balance in modern society?
What are the effects of stress on individuals and society?
Do you think a four-day working week is a good idea?
Who is more responsible for reducing workplace stress: employers or employees?
sampleAnswers: There are several possible explanations. Technology means work can follow us everywhere, so the working day doesn't really end when we leave the office. Many people also have more commitments outside work, such as long commutes, children's activities and social obligations. Economic pressures play a part too; in many cities, housing is so expensive that people take on extra work just to cover their costs. And there's a cultural element. Being busy is often seen as a sign of importance, so people may fill their time deliberately.

I think it's possible, but it's harder for some people than others. Professionals with flexible jobs and decent salaries can often arrange their schedules to make time for family and hobbies. However, people in low-paid jobs who need to work long hours or several jobs to make ends meet have far less choice. So while individuals can make some changes, such as setting boundaries around their working hours, a real balance often depends on wider factors like employment laws, wages and the cost of living.

For individuals, chronic stress can lead to serious physical and mental health problems, such as heart disease, insomnia, anxiety and depression. It can also damage relationships, as people under stress often have less patience and less time for their families. At a societal level, the costs are enormous. Stress-related illnesses lead to lost working days and higher healthcare spending, and burnout can drive skilled people out of their professions entirely, as we've seen with teachers and nurses in many countries.

I think it's an interesting idea that deserves serious consideration. Several trials have suggested that productivity often stays the same or even improves, because people are more rested and focused. It could also benefit families and reduce commuting. However, it might not work for every sector. In healthcare or retail, for example, services need to be available every day, so it would require hiring more staff, which could be costly. So perhaps it should be introduced gradually, starting in industries where it's most practical.

I'd say employers carry more responsibility, because they control the main causes of workplace stress, such as workload, deadlines and the general culture of the organisation. If a company expects employees to answer emails at midnight, there's only so much an individual can do. That said, employees also have a role to play, for instance by communicating clearly when they're overloaded and looking after their own wellbeing. Ideally, it should be a partnership, with employers creating healthy conditions and employees feeling able to speak up.

questions: On what occasions do people in your country give gifts?
Do you think expensive gifts are better than cheap ones?
Has the way people give gifts changed in recent years?
Why do some companies give gifts to their customers or employees?
Do you think people spend too much money on gifts during holidays?
sampleAnswers: The most common occasions are birthdays and the winter holidays, when families exchange presents. People also give gifts at weddings, often money, and when a baby is born. There are smaller traditions as well, such as bringing a bottle of wine or some dessert when you're invited to someone's home for dinner. In professional contexts, it's fairly common to give a small present to a colleague who's leaving, and children often give their teachers something at the end of the school year.

Not at all, in my opinion. The value of a gift depends much more on how much thought has gone into it than on how much it costs. A handwritten letter or a homemade present can mean far more than an expensive item chosen in a hurry. Expensive gifts can even make people feel uncomfortable, because they might feel obliged to give something of similar value in return. That said, I can understand that for special occasions, such as a significant anniversary, some people want to show their appreciation with something more valuable.

Yes, quite noticeably. Online shopping has made gift buying much more convenient, and many people now send presents directly to friends who live far away. Gift cards and money transfers have also become more common, which is practical but arguably less personal. Another trend is giving experiences rather than objects, such as concert tickets or cooking classes. And some people are becoming more environmentally conscious, choosing second-hand gifts or agreeing with friends and family not to exchange presents at all.

Mainly for strategic reasons. For customers, small gifts like free samples or birthday discounts are a form of marketing; they create a positive impression and encourage loyalty, so customers are more likely to return. For employees, gifts or bonuses at the end of the year can be a way of showing appreciation and boosting morale, which can improve motivation and reduce staff turnover. Of course, a gift alone won't make up for poor working conditions, but as a gesture it can help to build goodwill.

I think many people do, partly because of commercial pressure. Advertising and social media create the impression that you need to buy lots of expensive presents to show you care, and some families feel they have to keep up with what others are doing. This can lead to debt, particularly for families on low incomes. On top of that, many gifts end up unused, which is wasteful. I think it would be healthier if people agreed on spending limits or focused on spending time together rather than buying lots of things.

questions: What kinds of people become famous nowadays?
Do you think famous people should be role models for young people?
How is fame today different from fame in the past?
What are the disadvantages of being famous?
Do celebrities have a responsibility to speak out about social issues?
sampleAnswers: Nowadays, it seems almost anyone can become famous. Traditionally, fame came from achievements in fields like sport, music, film or politics. Now, thanks to social media, people can become well known simply for sharing their lives, opinions or skills online, and some influencers have bigger audiences than film stars. Reality television also creates celebrities very quickly. Scientists and activists can also become famous, although they rarely receive as much attention as entertainers, which I think says something about our priorities as a society.

Whether they like it or not, they are role models, because young people pay so much attention to them. So I think it's reasonable to expect them to behave responsibly, at least in public. However, it seems unfair to expect perfection; celebrities are human and will make mistakes. Parents and teachers should also encourage young people to look up to people in their own lives, or to admire specific qualities, like hard work or kindness, rather than idolising someone simply for being famous.

I'd say the biggest difference is that fame has become much more accessible but also more temporary. In the past, there were fewer channels, such as a handful of TV stations and newspapers, so becoming famous was difficult, but once you were, you often stayed famous for a long time. Now, social media allows people to become famous almost overnight, but attention moves on very quickly. Celebrities also communicate directly with fans now, which creates a sense of closeness that didn't exist when they were only seen on screen.

The most obvious one is the lack of privacy. Famous people are often followed by photographers and constantly recognised in public, which makes ordinary activities like going shopping quite stressful. Their mistakes are also magnified, and with social media, they can face intense criticism and even abuse from millions of strangers. This pressure can contribute to mental health problems, and there have been many sad examples of this. There's also the uncertainty: fame can disappear as quickly as it arrives, which must be difficult to cope with.

I think they have a great opportunity to raise awareness, given how many people listen to them, so it can be very positive when they use their platform for good causes. However, I'm not sure it's a responsibility. Celebrities aren't necessarily experts on complex social issues, and sometimes their comments can be poorly informed or even counterproductive. I'd say that if they choose to speak out, they should do their research first, but they shouldn't be criticised for preferring to stay out of politics.

questions: How has the internet changed the way people learn?
Do you think children should have limits on how much time they spend online?
What are the risks of sharing personal information online?
Should the internet be more strictly regulated?
Do you think people will spend even more time online in the future?
sampleAnswers: It's made learning far more accessible and flexible. Anyone with an internet connection can watch lectures from top universities, use language apps or find tutorials on almost any subject, often for free. This has been particularly valuable for people who can't attend traditional classes because of work, money or location. However, it's also created new challenges. There's so much information available that it can be hard to know what's reliable, and learning online requires a lot of self-discipline, which not everyone has.

Yes, I believe some limits are sensible, particularly for younger children. Spending too much time online can affect sleep, physical activity and concentration, and young children may be exposed to inappropriate content. That said, I think the focus should be on the type of activity rather than just the amount of time. An hour spent on an educational project is very different from an hour scrolling through videos. As children get older, it's probably more effective to teach them to manage their own time than to impose strict rules.

There are quite a few. The most serious is probably identity theft, where criminals use personal details to access bank accounts or make purchases. Personal information can also be used for scams that are very convincing because they include real details. Beyond that, companies collect and sell data to target advertising, often without users realising. And there are social risks too: something posted years ago can affect someone's job prospects, because once information is online, it's very difficult to remove completely.

I think some areas need more regulation, particularly regarding data protection, online harassment and the spread of dangerous misinformation. Large technology companies have enormous power, and it's reasonable for governments to hold them accountable. However, regulation has to be balanced carefully against freedom of expression. If rules are too strict, they could be used to censor legitimate opinions, which is a real risk in some countries. So I'd support clear, transparent rules focused on genuine harm, rather than broad controls over what people can say.

Probably, yes, as more aspects of daily life, such as work, shopping, healthcare and education, move online. Technologies like virtual reality might make online experiences even more immersive. However, I also think there could be a growing awareness of the downsides. Many people are already trying to limit their screen time, and some schools are banning phones. So while overall internet use will likely increase, I'd expect more people to make conscious efforts to protect time offline, for example by having phone-free meals or holidays.

questions: Why do adults decide to learn new skills?
Do you think children learn faster than adults?
Should employers pay for their employees to learn new skills?
Is it important for people to learn a second language?
How can society encourage more people to keep learning throughout their lives?
sampleAnswers: There are many motivations. For some, it's career-related; they need new skills to get a promotion, change jobs or keep up with changes in their industry. Others learn for personal reasons, such as wanting a new challenge or a hobby, especially after retirement or when their children have grown up. Some adults are motivated by social reasons, like wanting to meet new people. And sometimes it's practical, such as learning a language before moving abroad or learning to cook after leaving home.

In some areas, yes. Children seem to pick up languages and pronunciation more naturally, and they're often less afraid of making mistakes, which helps enormously. Their brains are also thought to be particularly adaptable. However, adults have certain advantages. They can use strategies, understand complex explanations and connect new information to what they already know. They're also often more motivated, because they've chosen to learn something. So I'd say children have the edge in some skills, but adults can learn very effectively too, given time and effort.

I think it's in employers' interests to do so, at least for skills related to the job. Training makes employees more productive, helps companies adapt to new technology, and can improve staff loyalty, since people tend to stay with employers who invest in them. On the other hand, small businesses may not be able to afford expensive training, so perhaps governments could help through subsidies. For skills unrelated to the job, I think it's reasonable for individuals to pay themselves, although some companies offer that as a benefit.

I'd say it's very valuable, although perhaps not essential for everyone. A second language opens up job opportunities, makes travelling easier, and allows you to communicate with people from different cultures, which can broaden your perspective. There's also some research suggesting that being bilingual has cognitive benefits, such as better problem-solving. For people whose first language is less widely spoken, learning an international language is almost a necessity. Even for native English speakers, though, I think learning another language shows respect for other cultures.

One important step would be to make learning more affordable and flexible, for example through free online courses, evening classes at local colleges and government-funded training vouchers. Employers could also allow time for training during working hours. I think attitudes matter too. If learning is seen as something you only do when you're young, adults may feel embarrassed about starting something new. Public campaigns or simply celebrating adult learners could help change that. Libraries and community centres could also play a bigger role as local learning hubs.
